planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; broad-leaved toad lily blooms earlier in summer than most Tricyrtis species and its arching stems benefit from the support of nearby ferns or shrubs.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; broad-leaved toad lily blooms earlier in summer than most Tricyrtis species and its arching stems benefit from the support of nearby ferns or shrubs. Tricyrtis latifolia is an East Asian woodland species with broad, glossy, clasping leaves along arching stems, topped and lined along the upper leaf axils with clusters of pale yellow flowers heavily speckled with purple-brown spots in early to midsummer, earlier than most other toad lilies bloom. Its early flowering extends the toad lily season in a shaded border, pairing well with later-blooming Tricyrtis hirta selections for a longer overall display. Give it consistent moisture and rich soil, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yellow toad lily has clear unspeckled flowers unlike most spotted Tricyrtis species and makes a bright accent among darker-flowered woodland perennials.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yellow toad lily has clear unspeckled flowers unlike most spotted Tricyrtis species and makes a bright accent among darker-flowered woodland perennials. Tricyrtis flava is a Japanese woodland species notable among toad lilies for its clean, unspotted, soft yellow, upward-facing flowers held along and atop upright stems in mid to late summer, a departure from the heavily speckled purple-and-white flowers typical of the genus. Its bright, uncluttered flower color and more compact habit make it a good choice for brightening a shaded corner or pairing with spotted toad lily species for color contrast. It performs best with the same consistently moist, humus-rich conditions favored by hosta and Solomon's seal, and divides readily in spring.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Thunberg's jack-in-the-pulpit has unusually long, thread-like extensions trailing from its hooded spathe, a distinctive feature best appreciated planted where it can be viewed up close.

directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Thunberg's jack-in-the-pulpit has unusually long, thread-like extensions trailing from its hooded spathe, a distinctive feature best appreciated planted where it can be viewed up close. Arisaema thunbergii is a Japanese woodland aroid with glossy, divided, umbrella-like leaves and a dark purple-black to green hooded flower (spathe) in spring, drawn out into a remarkably long, whip-like tail that can trail six inches or more beyond the hood — one of the most dramatic flower forms among cultivated Arisaema. It is a choice specialty plant for a shaded woodland or collector's garden, best massed with other Arisaema species and woodland ephemerals for a layered spring display, followed by a spike of bright red berries in fall. Like other Arisaema, all plant parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are irritating if chewed, so site away from areas where pets or children might sample the showy berries.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Korean epimedium is more cold-hardy than many barrenworts and spreads at a moderate rate to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover under deciduous trees.

directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Korean epimedium is more cold-hardy than many barrenworts and spreads at a moderate rate to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover under deciduous trees. Epimedium koreanum is native to Korea and northeastern China, forming a low, semi-evergreen to deciduous mound of heart-shaped, spiny-edged leaflets that emerge bronze-tinged in spring before turning green, with airy sprays of pale yellow to white, spurred flowers held just above the foliage in early to mid-spring. It is among the most cold-tolerant epimedium species available, making it a dependable groundcover choice for northern shade gardens where less hardy Asian species may struggle, and it has also been used medicinally in traditional Korean and Chinese herbalism. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to fully display the spring bloom.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; unlike the North American mayapple, Chinese mayapple is evergreen to semi-evergreen in mild climates and does not go dormant by midsummer.

Podophyllum pleianthum is a bold Asian relative of the familiar native mayapple, with large, glossy, deeply lobed, umbrella-like leaves held on sturdy stems and clusters of dark maroon-red, drooping flowers hidden beneath the foliage in spring, followed by large orange-red fruit. Its substantial, architectural leaves and persistent foliage make it a striking textural specimen for a shaded border or woodland garden, holding interest through more of the season than the spring-ephemeral American species. Give it rich, evenly moist soil and protection from harsh winter wind at the cooler end of its range, and divide the slowly spreading rhizome in fall to propagate.
